newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia backs telecom pact, but offers little.
newsitem.headline: Asia backs telecom pact, but offers little.

text.p: Ten Asian nations have backed a historic pact to open the US$600 billion global telecomunications market, but their meagre contributions show change in the region will be slow, analysts said on Monday.

Sixty-eight members of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) agreed at the weekend to measures that will lower telecommunications costs for consumers, increase global competition and stimulate the world economy.

Japan, Australia, Singapore, the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, South Korea, Papua New Guinea and Brunei signed the pact, which marked the culmination of three years of tortuous negotiations.

"The impact will be more muted (in Asia) than in the European Union or the U.S. because various (Asian) markets did not put as much on the table as they did," said Dan Sherman, an analyst at Salomon Brothers.
Indonesia and Malaysia offered nothing new, while Thailand and South Korea are among countries which will maintain limits on foreign participation in their markets, analysts said.
"Malaysia has not agreed to change anything that it has already agreed to," said a telecommunications analyst at a foreign equity research house in Kuala Lumpur.
The ceiling on foreign ownership in Malaysian telecoms firms would remain at 30 percent.

WTO Director-General Renato Ruggerio and U.S. President Bill Clinton hailed the pact as good news for the global marketplace. The United States has the largest share of the market with just under 30 percent of total revenue.
Japan, with the third largest share of the market at 15.6 percent, agreed to remove long-standing foreign equity limits on most carriers and radio-based services.

But it kept a foreign equity ceiling of 20 percent on its two telecommunications giants, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT) and Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co (KDD), much to the annoyance of the United States.
Washington is likely to keep pressing Tokyo to remove those limits, something NTT believes will happen eventually.
"In future there will probably be a trend in countries including Japan to remove such restrictions, and we expect them ultimately to be removed," an NTT spokesman said.
Reactions to the impact the agreement would have on other Asian countries were as diverse as the nations themselves.
Analysts said the pact was not likely to have much direct impact on Hong Kong companies, but said it did suggest opportunities would open up when China joined the WTO.
"I think Hong Kong operators would be seen as obvious beneficiaries if that happens," said David Gibbons, regional telecoms analyst at HSBC James Capel.
China, which will resume control of Hong Kong on July 1, currently bans foreign equity participation in domestic telecom service providers.
Some Asian countries, such as Indonesia, are pursuing plans to develop infrastructure for the industry, so any change will be at their own pace, Sherman at Salomon Brothers said.
Others, such as Singapore and the Philippines, already have embarked on liberalising their telecommunication markets.

"With or without the pact, Singapore is going ahead to liberalise the telecom sector because it wants to be a business centre and attract more multinationals here," said Chan Wai Tien, an analyst at J.M. Sassoon in Singapore.
"Its most likely impact is an overcrowded industry. There will be too many players in some telecom sectors," Saturnino Mejia, research head at Guoco Securities in Manila, said of the Philippines.
South Korea will continue to limit foreign participation, but analysts see possible joint ventures or mergers and acquisitions.
